deep.reconstruction:
The page continues a table of quadratic residues modulo primes. The previous page covers 181 to 229 and the next page continues 271, then 277 onward. There is no derivation on the page, only tabulated data. Each entry has the same layout.

(a) The prime p is written in the margin with a sign above it: '+' for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and '—' for p ≡ 3 (mod 4).

(b) For p ≡ 1 (mod 4) (here 233, 241, 257, 269) the list carries the sign ∓ (or ±). It gives only the residues r with 0 < r < p/2. Since (−1/p) = +1, the residues come in pairs ±r, so this half determines all of them. Each such list must have (p−1)/4 entries. I counted: 233 gives 58, 241 gives 60, 257 gives 64, 269 gives 67. All are correct.

(c) For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (here 239, 251, 263, 271) the list carries the sign '+'. It gives all residues in 1..p−1, which is (p−1)/2 of them, because −1 is a non-residue. I counted 239 in full: 119 entries, correct. The list for 271 runs past the end of the page, to 268 on the next page.

(d) For 257 and 269 Gauss draws vertical strokes in the list.
- For 257 they fall at 32|34, 64|67 and 95|98.
- For 269 they fall at 30|34, 67|70 and 100|103.
- These are exactly the points p/8, p/4 and 3p/8.
- The same pattern appears on the previous page for 181, 197 and 229.

So Gauss is dividing (0, p/2) into octants and counting residues in each. My counts (mine, not on the page):
- p = 269: octant counts 15, 24, 15, 13 (sum 67). That gives 39 residues against 28 non-residues in (0, p/4).
- p = 257: octant counts 20, 16, 12, 16 (sum 64). That gives 36 residues against 28 non-residues in (0, p/4).

Such octant and quarter counts are what enter class-number relations of Dirichlet type for forms of determinant −p and −2p. For p ≡ 1 (mod 4) the relation is h(−4p) = 2·Σ_{0<n<p/4} (n/p). This plausibly explains the purpose of the strokes; my reading of their purpose is inference.

I spot-checked many entries by quadratic reciprocity, for example:
- 233: 2, 7 and 13 are residues; 3 is a non-residue.
- 241: 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19 are absent; 47, 53, 59 and 61 are present.
- 239: 11, 17, 29 and 31 are present; 7, 13, 19, 23 and 37 are absent.
- 251, 263 and 271: various entries, all consistent.

Gauss's own overwritten corrections are all right:
- 150 (not 149) in 239;
- 9 and 20 (not 19) in 241;
- 103 in 271;
- 124, 225, 240 and 81.
errors: No genuine errors found in the residue lists that were checked.
Gauss's corrections (239: 150 replacing 149; 241: inserted 9, and 20 replacing 19; 271: 103) are all mathematically correct.

In the 263 list the machine transcription reads '171', but 171 = 9·19 and (19/263) = −1, so 171 is a non-residue. 172 = 4·43 is a residue, since (43/263) = 1, and also 172 ≡ −91 with 91 a non-residue. The manuscript glyph is overwritten and is most likely 172, so this is a transcription error rather than Gauss's.

results.usually_credited_to: Standard tables (Legendre, Gauss Disquisitiones table, later Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus 1839)

results.what: Division of the residue list at p/8, p/4 and 3p/8 to count residues per octant (strokes for 257 and 269, and for 181, 197, 229 on the previous page).
results.modern_name: Counting quadratic residues in intervals (0, kp/8); class-number formulas of Dirichlet type, e.g. h(−4p) = 2·Σ_{n<p/4} (n/p)
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1839) for the proven formulas; Gauss's empirical knowledge of class-number relations is documented in his Nachlass (Werke II)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational residue table. The octant markers suggest class-number or residue-distribution counting, which is already known from Gauss's Nachlass. There is nothing new beyond confirming the purpose and the care of the table.

239 list: the overwritten entry is 150 (replacing 149), correctly shown as the superscript '150'.
241 list: the superscript '9' and '20' are insertions or overwrites, giving ...8.9.10... and ...18.20.24...; '19' is deleted.
The vertical strokes in the 257 list (after 32, 64, 95) and the 269 list (after 30, 67, 100) are omitted in the transcription. They mark p/8, p/4 and 3p/8.
